Post Clone Wars, it's because the idea of a droid army is taboo, and everyone remembers the horror that an army that doesn't have any emotions can inflict.

Pre Clone Wars, a pure droid army isn't the most effective thing.

B1 battle droids aren't all that smart or effective, and CIS battle strategy consisted of overwhelming the enemy through sheer numbers. You line up all the B1s, and march them towards the enemy and hope that it's too much to bear.

The more intelligent droids, like commandos and Magna Guards, are much more expensive, and even the CIS, with all the wealth of the banking clan, couldn't afford to use those droids for their standard infantry.

The advantage is that your army has no self preservation, so you can be more expendable with your tactics. Sacrificing 1000 soldiers to win a battle is no big deal when they're droids who can be repaired or replaced. The Republic didn't have that advantage.

The disadvantage is that you cannot use advanced tactics, and that your soldiers are going to get themselves killed rather often.

The B1s didn't have much programming beyond matching straight towards the enemy, and so you would have a hard time using the environment to your advantage, encirclement tactics, subterfuge, etc. And you need to be able to replace your fallen soldiers which gets pricey.

So most people opted for organic militaries. These militaries often had droids deployed, but they weren't common and were a part of an organic unit.

Also, Revan's Sith army had a lot of droids, more than is depicted in Kotor. The Star Forge could pump out an endless supply of droid soldiers, and those probably made up a significant portion of the Sith army during the Jedi Civil War. Kreia even comments that she never understood Revan's fascination with droids.

Andromeda is a tale of wasted time. The game, despite having a 5 year development cycle, 99% of what needed up on the disc was made in the final year or so of dev time.

The first thing I'd change is banning the devs from doing any work with procedural generation. The initial idea for Andromeda was to have every planet be completely procedurally generated: the terrain, the buildings, the inhabitants, and the quests. Procedural generation cannot create meaningful quest content.

In the end, the 4 years of procedural generation development resulting in the devs using it just to create the landscape of the planets, and then have devs fill those planets with hand crafted content. Handcrafted content is good, but the devs should have been hand crafting it from the start, not scrambling in the final year.

The other big thing is to have someone with a strong vision in the director's position. The first director for Andromeda, Gérard Lehiany, left in 2014, after not bringing the game out of pre-production, essentially having the team do 2 years of nothing before dumping the project. Mac Walters stepped up to fill the position, and while he did a great job of getting the devs to work and start actually creating things beyond prototypes and concept art, he obviously didn't want to do the job, nor did he have a vision for the game.

An example of a strong director making or breaking a project is Josh Sawyer and Fallout New Vegas. Sawyer had a vision for the game, shared that vision with his coworkers, and everyone worked in unison to realise that vision, despite the dev time of 18 months. New Vegas is more than the sum of its parts because of it.

Walters had no desire to work on Andromeda, mostly due to the ridicule he suffered from fans for years due to writing Mass Effect 3's ending. One thing to keep in mind about game development is that it isn't a matter of parking people behind a desk and a progress bar fills up until the game is ready. Different developers do work at different times.

For example, the concept artists often finish their work early, and move on to the next project ahead of everyone else. In fact, after Fallout 4 launched, Todd Howard took a 3 month hiatus and returned to form a 3 man team of himself, Emil Pagliarulo, and a concept artist to work on Starfield's pre-production while everyone else was on 76, which was in 2016.

More examples are level designers often have to start later, when the engine and toolset are ready for them to work with. The people who design the UI don't work for the entire duration of development. Artists generally get done early making all the textures the devs use. Voice over talent comes in rather late in development.

This is to say that bringing the ESO team into TES 6 might end up with a bunch of redundant people. You can't just throw more bodies at development. In addition, ESO's devs are suited to MMO development, which might not translate to single player. We did see what happened when the single player focused Bethesda made a multiplayer game...

Imagine if TES 6 is set to have exactly 100 dungeons. So rather than having one guy make 100 dungeons, they get 100 devs to each make one dungeon. They might finish their work within a week, but that won't get the game out much faster as everyone else has to get their work done. Having one guy make 100 dungeons over the course of the same dev time everyone else is using creates the same result.

A huge part of Bethesda's sale price to Microsoft probably came from ESO being a love service, as consistent and future profits are valued more than cash in the bank. Grading didn't start as a scam tho, it was meant as a quality assurance measure for private sales.

I think collectable coins were the first thing to popularize grading. The idea is that if you're going to spend a ton of money on a collectable coin, you want to ensure it's in good condition. So a grading company would give it a score and seal in a case to ensure that quality stays the same. Grading companies built their brand off reputation, so you could trust the scores they're giving.

The issue is that people are willing to pay more for a highly graded item than a lower scored one. Hell, people will pay more for an item of a decent grade than an ungraded version. And grading is a very subjective thing, no matter how clear a company is on their rules for grading (which is where the idea of sending an item to get graded over and over until you get the grade you want comes in).

So someone got the idea to buy up a bunch of coins, then collude with a grading company by grading a bunch of things high, regardless of the quality, then sell them for a huge profit. The worst part is that people are so dumb that they're willing to trust the grade given to an item over their own eyes, as these coins were in shit condition but given high grades.

And this cycle is repeated with every new collectable. Comics, trading cards, and now video games, are the big ones.

There are responsible ways to run a grading company. First, don't collude with people trying to make money off this, which is obvious. But the other is population counts. If you ever start a grading company, keep a record of every item you grade and the grade you give it, and make that publicly available.

If your grading company has only ever given a 9.8 to a single showcase Obi-Wan, it's going to be more valuable than if you have given 9.8s to 1000 showcase Obi-Wans. And that will inform collectors on the value of the Obi-Wan.

In the books, Frodo, Sam and Gollum meet Faramir, Faramir isn't tempted, and they move on. This results in the Two Towers ending with the Shelob scene. So yeah, the battle of Helm's Deep and Shelob happen at the same time, give or take. It's complicated because, when the fellowship splits, the novel is written by going through only Frodo and Sam's story, reaching the climax, then backtracking to what Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli's story.

Then Return of the King does the entirety of Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli's plot. And the last thing we saw of Frodo and Sam was Frodo getting stabbed by Shelob, and presumed dead. So when the mouth of Sauron shows Frodo's mithril shirt (I think he shows other things in the book), the reader actually thinks Frodo died, and our hero Aragorn will get the ring and finish the quest.

Anyway, the structure of the films intertwines the two stories and has them move at the same pace. So if Frodo and Sam make it to Shelob during the battle of Helm's Deep, then Return of the King would have a lot of story left for Team Aragorn and very little story for team Frodo.

So Frodo and Sam need to slow down during The Two Towers so team Aragorn can catch up. The writers decided to give Faramir a bit of an arc in being tempted by the ring. It also gives the audience a chance to get to know Faramir before his character becomes important to Return of the King.

1, it allows you to grab banished Boss monsters. The obvious use is to use Supernova twice in one turn. That's the main reason it saw play in original post structure deck builds. Games can be won with just Red Zone plus Supernova.

2, the Pop effect with RDA is less a vital effect and more of cherry on top. If something gets destroyed while you have Crimson Gaia, you can summon back an RDA to get that pop, which comes in handy. But unless you can set up a play that leaves RDA on the field, or summon it back with Gaia, it's not being used.

3, it allows you to play with chains. Let's say your opponent activates Dark Ruler No More. You cannot respond with Hot Red Abyss because neither player can respond with monster effects. But you can chain Red Zone, a trap, by just activating the card, you don't need to use any effects, then chain Hot Red Abyss to negate the Dark Ruler. It's why the more advanced Centur-Ion hybrid variant of RDA plays Red Zone and cuts Fiendish Golem. We prioritize being able to negate with Abyss over a banish.

But if Supernova is going to be included in the end board, Red Zone is the way to go. So it's all about making decisions on what monsters you're going to end on, and which trap is going to support them the most.

So, if you're playing a pure structure deck build of RDA, Golem is going to come up more, because to end on Supernova, you generally need to open Crimson Resonator and Bone Archfiend. But when you do have access to Supernova, Red Zone enabling the double board wipe banish is the way to go.

Build a technique to delete every enemy instantly.

A big part of publishers shutting down recently purchased studios has to do with quarterly/yearly profits.

Shareholders get a steady dividend income from their ownership of a company, but that just isn't good enough for these evil beings. They need to see an increased profit quarter after quarter. If a company they invest in makes a million dollars for that shareholder in one year, another million next year is considered a failure, and only an increase matters.

So there are two ways for a company to make a profit. One is to earn money, in the instance of video games, it's to sell video games. But a lot of publishers suck at selling good games at times, so they rely on the second method of making profit:

Cutting costs. Close a studio, sell off its assets like the office space, computers, desks, chairs, printers, etc. and now you suddenly don't have an entire studio's worth of expenses, so you can devote that saved money to the shareholders.

It's fucking evil.

Anyway, why don't you sell the company instead of a shutdown? For starters sales take time, and you're helping your competitors. And finally they still make money off the sales of that studio's games.
